label: Outside witness
knownFor: A Roman biographer of the emperors, who notes that Claudius expelled Jews stirred up by "Chrestus" and that Nero punished the Christians.
shortDescription: Suetonius was a Roman scholar who wrote the lives of Rome's rulers from Julius Caesar to Domitian. In them, two short lines tell of Jews driven from Rome under Claudius for rioting at the urging of Chrestus, and of punishments laid on the Christians under Nero.
datesNote: No old source gives the year of his birth or his death. He says he was a young man twenty years after Nero's death, so about 88. His lives end with Domitian, who died in 96, so he wrote after that. He later ran the emperor Hadrian's letters.

keyWorks.title: Lives of the Caesars

keyWorks.title: On Illustrious Men
keyWorks.about: lives of Rome's men of letters, which survive only in part. Jerome followed its example for his short lives of Christian writers

traces: About 725, Bede set down the Claudius line in his chronicle of the world almost in Suetonius's words, without Chrestus. He put it in Claudius's ninth year and added that Luke also reports it, joining it to the Acts of the Apostles.

Jerome wrote short lives of Christian writers, up to the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius. He says he was asked to follow the example of Tranquillus, and to do for Christian writers what Suetonius had done for the men of letters among the pagans.
In the preface to his chronicle, Jerome says he gathered much for the years from Troy to Constantine from Tranquillus and other historians.
remembered: About 200, Tertullian of Carthage names Suetonius twice. He sends his readers to him on which games were founded for which gods, and cites him for the report that Nero never dreamed, except with difficulty at the very end of his life. He never cites the line on the Christians.
Tertullian complained that pagans called Christians Chrestians, and Lactantius, later, that the ignorant called Christ Chrestus. Neither names Suetonius.

Thierry Ruinart, a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés who died in 1709, used both lines against Henry Dodwell's dissertation on the fewness of martyrs, printed at Oxford in 1684. Ruinart read the Jews whom Claudius drove out as including Christians. Because Suetonius lists the punishment among Nero's measures, Ruinart judged that Nero must have issued a written order against the Christians. Suetonius names no such order.

uncertain: Who Chrestus was. Suetonius does not say who Chrestus was, or where he was. The name is close in sound to Christus, the Latin form of Christ. Lactantius says the ignorant call Christ Chrestus by changing one letter, and Tertullian says pagans call Christians Chrestians. Neither of them names Suetonius.
Chrestus as a name. It was also a real name. Eusebius copies a letter from the emperor Constantine to Chrestus, bishop of Syracuse.
All the Jews. The Latin of the Claudius line says only Jews. It has no word for all, and none for one before Chrestus. The Acts of the Apostles says Claudius ordered all the Jews to leave Rome.

Driven out, or barred from meeting. Suetonius and Acts both say the Jews left Rome. Dio, a later Roman historian, is held here only in a badly damaged print of his Greek. As far as it can be read, he says Claudius did not drive the Jews out, but ordered them not to gather.
The year. Neither Suetonius nor Acts gives a year for the expulsion. Bede, writing about 725, puts it in the ninth year of Claudius's reign.
The same event. Neither Suetonius nor Acts says that it tells of the same order as the other. Bede joins them, adding that Luke also reports it.
The punishment under Nero. Suetonius names no charge, no number, no kind of punishment and no law. He files it among Nero's acts that, he says, deserve no blame, and some even praise.
Suetonius blames Nero for the great fire, but his notice of the Christians does not mention it.
Superstition. Suetonius calls the Christians' faith a new and harmful superstition, his word for a religion he despised. In his life of Claudius, the Druids' rite in Gaul is a religion.
Suetonius names the Christians only once, in his life of Nero.

The dismissal. A life of Hadrian written long after says that Hadrian replaced Suetonius, Septicius Clarus, the commander of his guard, and many others. The reason it gives is that they had behaved toward his wife Sabina, without his leave, more familiarly than the respect owed to the court allowed. No other old source tells of it.

Rolfe: the people of old Troy freed from tax forever as founders of the Roman race; the Jews driven from Rome for rioting at the urging of Chrestus; the German envoys allowed to sit with the senators at the theater.

Nero 19.3: these acts deserve no blame, some even praise. Nero 38: Nero set Rome on fire.
Otho 10.1, Nero 57.2 and Domitian 12.2: his father an army officer; Suetonius a young man under Domitian. The lives run from Julius Caesar to Domitian.

quotationOriginals.modern: He drove out of Rome the Jews who kept rioting at the urging of Chrestus.
quotationOriginals.printed: Iudaeos impulsore Chresto assidue tumultuantis Roma expulit.
quotationOriginals.work: Suetonius, Lives of the Caesars, Claudius 25.4, Latin, with tr. John C. Rolfe (1914)
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: Since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, he expelled them from Rome.
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Latin has no word for "since", "all" or "one". Rolfe adds "since"; the Thomson and Forester English adds "all" and "one".

quotationOriginals.work: Tertullian, To the Nations 1.3, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3; Latin ed. Reifferscheid and Wissowa (1890)

quotationOriginals.modern: Punishments were laid on the Christians, a kind of people holding a new and harmful superstition.
quotationOriginals.printed: afflicti suppliciis Christiani, genus hominum superstitionis novae ac maleficae
quotationOriginals.work: Suetonius, Lives of the Caesars, Nero 16.2, Latin, with tr. John C. Rolfe (1914)
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: Punishment was inflicted on the Christians, a class of men given to a new and mischievous superstition.
quotationOriginals.uncertain: For maleficae Rolfe has "mischievous" and the Thomson and Forester English "impious". The modern English says "harmful". The Latin has no verb with Nero as its subject: punishments were laid on the Christians, under him.

quotationOriginals.modern: You say it wrong, and call us 'Chrestians', for you are not even clearly sure of the name itself. Even so, it rings of sweetness or goodness.
quotationOriginals.printed: etiam  cum  corrupte  a uobis Chrestiani  pronuntiamur  (nam  ne  no|minis  quidem  ipsius  liquido certi  estis),  sic  quoque  de  suauitate  uel  boni|tate  modulatum est.
quotationOriginals.work: Tertullian, To the Nations 1.3, Latin, ed. August Reifferscheid and Georg Wissowa (1890)
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: Even when by a faulty pronunciation you call us “Chrestians” (for you are not certain about even the sound of this noted name), you in fact lisp out the sense of pleasantness and goodness.
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The modern English is made from the Latin. The vertical strokes and the double spaces stand in the printed Latin as the Library holds it. Tertullian makes the same point in his Apology 3, where the Ante-Nicene English adds "the name you hate".

timeline.when: Under Claudius, in the first century
timeline.headline: Jews driven from Rome

lines.text: Claudius frees the people of old Troy from tax forever, because, Suetonius says, they founded the Roman race.
Claudius drives from Rome the Jews who, Suetonius says, kept rioting at the urging of Chrestus. Suetonius does not say who Chrestus was.
Claudius lets German envoys sit with the senators at the theater.
At Corinth, the apostle Paul meets Aquila, a Jew, and his wife Priscilla, lately come from Italy because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome.
lines.reference: The Acts of the Apostles 18:1-2, cic/texts/webbe_world-english-bible-british-edition.xml lines 88521-88524
lines.note: This is the Acts of the Apostles, in the New Testament. Neither Acts nor Suetonius says that both tell of the same order.

timeline.when: Under Nero, in the first century
timeline.headline: Punishments laid on the Christians
timeline.witness: Suetonius, in his life of Nero

lines.text: Many abuses, Suetonius says, are severely punished and put down, and new rules made. Spending is limited, and taverns are barred from selling cooked food except beans and greens.

Punishments are laid on the Christians, whom Suetonius calls a kind of people holding a new and harmful superstition, his word for a religion he despised. He names no charge, number or kind of punishment.
The chariot drivers are stopped from roaming the streets and cheating and robbing people for fun.
Suetonius files these among Nero's acts that deserve no blame, and some even praise, before he turns to Nero's crimes.
Suetonius says Nero himself set Rome on fire. In that chapter he names no Christians.

timeline.when: From Otho's war to the reign of Hadrian
timeline.headline: The writer's own life

lines.text: His father, Suetonius Laetus, an officer in the Thirteenth legion, takes part in the war.

lines.when: Twenty years after Nero's death, so about 88
lines.text: Suetonius is a young man when a man of unknown birth appears, claiming to be Nero.
In his youth, Suetonius is present at a hearing before a Roman official and a crowded court.
He writes the lives of twelve rulers of Rome, from Julius Caesar to Domitian.
lines.reference: Suetonius, Lives of the Caesars, from the life of Julius to the life of Domitian, cic/texts/suetonius_lives-of-the-caesars-loeb_rolfe1914.txt lines 918-41018

lines.text: He runs the emperor Hadrian's letters, until Hadrian replaces him.
lines.note: This rests on a life of Hadrian written long after.

timeline.headline: Christian readers, and a name said wrong

lines.text: At Carthage, Tertullian sends his readers to Suetonius Tranquillus on which games were founded for which gods.
Tertullian cites Suetonius for the report that Nero never dreamed, except with difficulty at the very end of his life.

In his appeal to the pagans, Tertullian says the name Christian comes from anointing. He tells them they say it wrong and call Christians Chrestians, and that even so it rings of sweetness or goodness. He does not name Suetonius.
lines.note: In Greek, chrestos means good or kind. Tertullian makes the same point in his Apology 3.

lines.text: Lactantius writes that Christ is a title of power and rule, not a proper name, since the Jews called their kings by it. He says the ignorant call Christ Chrestus by changing one letter. He explains that the Jews anointed their priests and kings with holy oil, so Christ means the anointed one. He does not name Suetonius.

timeline.headline: Bede carries the Claudius line on

lines.text: In his chronicle of the world, Bede sets down the Claudius line almost in Suetonius's words, without Chrestus. He puts it in Claudius's ninth year and adds that Luke also reports it.

timeline.headline: A monk reads both lines against a scholar
timeline.witness: Thierry Ruinart, a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés

lines.text: Ruinart answers Henry Dodwell's dissertation on the fewness of martyrs, printed at Oxford in 1684.
Ruinart reads the Jews whom Claudius drove out as including Christians.
Because Suetonius lists the punishment among Nero's measures, Ruinart judges that Nero must have issued a written order against the Christians.
Ruinart dies of a fever.
